transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Yeah, uh… I came in because I’m having a hard time keeping my attention where it needs to be. Like at work, I’ll start a safety briefing or we’re going over a plan review, and I’m really trying to listen — I know it matters — but within a few minutes my head is already on three other job problems.

Then I miss stuff I absolutely should’ve caught. And in construction, you know, that’s not like forgetting what you walked into a room for… although I do that too sometimes—sorry, anyway. It’s the safety stuff and plan details that worry me. I’ll be standing there looking like I’m following along, but my mind has already run off somewhere else.
When you think back to childhood, were problems with attention already there?

Yeah, they were. I mean, I didn’t think of it that way back then, obviously, I was just a kid, but in elementary school my teachers were already telling my parents stuff like I couldn’t stay in my seat, I was talking when I wasn’t supposed to, losing homework all the time.

And I’d do this thing where I’d rush through the directions before I really understood what they wanted. Like I’d just start doing the worksheet or whatever and then realize I did half of it wrong. My mom used to get those notes from school, and—yeah, sorry, I’m kind of jumping around—but yes, it was definitely there when I was little.
Do you have the same trouble paying attention outside of work, like at home or in everyday conversations?

Yeah, yeah, it happens at home too. Like my foreman will be talking straight to me, or my wife will be telling me something, and I’m looking right at them — like I’m not ignoring them on purpose — but then I realize I only caught the last few words.

So I’ll have to say, “Sorry, run that by me again,” which… my wife hates that, understandably. And then sometimes I try to piece together what they said from the part I did hear, but that doesn’t really work. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I know it looks like I don’t care.
Do you often feel excessively worried or on edge, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to deal with?

Um… excessively worried? I don’t know. I mean, I worry when there’s something actually going on, like if a job is behind or there’s a safety issue, but just sitting around feeling on edge for no reason… I’m not sure I’d say that.

I guess I’d have to think about what you mean by “on edge,” because my mind is busy a lot, but I don’t know if that’s worry exactly.
Do you often feel restless, like it’s hard to sit still?

Yeah. I mean, sitting still is… not my strong suit. Like in meetings, when everyone else is just sitting there through the whole thing, I’m usually the guy who’s standing up, going to get coffee, stepping outside to “check something,” whatever excuse I can find to move around.

And it’s not even always that I need anything, you know? I’ll just feel like I’ve got to get up. Like if I sit there too long I start getting uncomfortable in my own skin. Sorry, I know that’s probably more than you asked, but yeah, it happens a lot.
Do you often blurt things out or interrupt people before they’ve finished speaking?

Yeah, I do that. I’ll cut people off because I think I already know where they’re going with it, you know? Like they start asking something and I’m already answering in my head, and then it comes out before they’re even done.

And then sometimes I realize, oh, they were actually about to add the important part, and I answered the wrong thing. That happens with guys on the job too — someone’s explaining an issue and I jump in with a solution, and then they’re like, “No, that’s not what I meant.” It’s not me trying to be rude, but… yeah, I do it.
When your concentration is bad, do you also feel down or depressed?

I don’t know if I’d call it depressed. When I can’t concentrate, I get frustrated, definitely. Like I’ll be trying to read through something or answer emails and then I realize I’ve been staring at the same thing for ten minutes, and that makes me irritated.

But “down” like sad or depressed… I’m not sure. I mean, sometimes it kind of ruins my mood, because then I’m behind and I start thinking about everything I didn’t get done, and then—sorry, I’m going off. I guess I haven’t really noticed it as depression exactly.
Do you often feel sleepy during the day?

Sleepy? Uh… I don’t know, not really something I’ve paid attention to. I mean, I get tired like anyone else, especially if it’s been a long day, but sleepy during the day like I’m nodding off? I’m not sure.

Sometimes after lunch I’ll feel kind of blah, but then everybody on site complains about that, especially if it’s hot out or you ate something heavy. Sorry, that’s probably not what you’re asking. I guess I haven’t noticed being unusually sleepy, no.
Have these attention problems caused serious problems for you at work or at home?

Yeah… I mean, I’d like to say it’s just annoying, but it’s caused real problems.

At work it’s gotten bad. Like, if I miss a follow-up or I don’t keep the site coordination straight, it’s not just me being behind — other people are waiting on it, crews get mixed up, and then it turns into a whole thing. My employer has actually brought it up formally, like it’s a concern now, not just “try to do better.”

And at home… yeah. My wife is pretty worn out from having to remind me about stuff I already said I’d handle. I’ll tell her I’ve got it, and then it just… doesn’t happen, or I forget until she’s upset. I know that gets old for her.
When a task is really interesting or urgent, can you stay focused on it for a long time?

Sometimes, yeah, if it’s really on fire, like something urgent on the job, I can lock in for a bit. But honestly, what brings me in is more that I’ll start something important—like a safety briefing or a plan review—and I’m trying hard to pay attention, I really am, and then within a few minutes my head’s already jumped to three other job problems.

Like I’ll be thinking about a delivery, or whether a crew is where they’re supposed to be, or some issue from yesterday, and then I miss something I should’ve caught. And then later I’m like, how did I not hear that? So urgency helps some, but it doesn’t mean I can reliably stay with it.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports ADHD, combined presentation: persistent symptoms of both inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity were present since childhood, occur across work and home settings, and cause clinically significant functional impairment. The patient specifically confirms multiple inattentive symptoms (difficulty sustaining attention, distractibility, seeming not to listen, losing homework in childhood, rushing through directions/careless errors) and multiple hyperactive/impulsive symptoms (could not stay seated in childhood, current restlessness/fidgety need to move, interrupting/blurting out). This is more specific than unspecified ADHD.
